name: Aaron Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an apprentice with a private line contractor. The power company hires us for the grunt work, mostly swapping old wooden poles for new ones and hooking up new housing estates on the edge of town. I run the auger truck a lot, set poles, frame them, and the journeymen do the hot work while I watch and learn. It's honest work, and the pay's better than the factory I was at before.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you leave the factory?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The money and the boredom, in that order. Here I'm outside, every street is different, and at the end of the week I've got more in my pocket than I know what to do with. I rent a cheap flat above my aunt's garage and my pickup's paid off, so I've got about seven months of pay sitting in the bank. I write everything in a little paper notebook, measurements, pole numbers, the lot; the guys rib me about it but it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say not much, to be honest. Maybe something like, see, all that fuss for nothing. I don't go online much, so it'd be a shrug at the truck at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's what I expected. I don't use the AI stuff, nobody on my crew really does, and poles still need setting. I write everything in a little paper notebook, and in this world nobody's going to take the notebook off me. The estates keep going up, so the work keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going like now: finish my apprenticeship in two and a half years, keep the pickup running, keep the money in the bank. Maybe I'd start looking at a small place to buy instead of renting from my aunt. Nothing fancy, a one-bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, even. I like it when things stay the way they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the biggest thing on your mind in this world, if it isn't AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Interest rates, probably, if I want to buy. And whether the contractor keeps winning the power company's tenders, because if they lose the big contract, we're scrambling. But there's three other contractors in town who'd hire me, so I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the notebook. Would anyone push you to change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office keeps asking us to use the tablet for job sign-off. I do it at the end of the day, copying from the notebook. It's slower but I trust paper.

I'd keep it to the **lunch truck**; I barely go online.
think: Privately it's what he expected, because **poles still need setting** whatever the computers do.
New **housing estates** on the edge of town keep the contractor's work coming.
do: Finish his **apprenticeship** in two and a half years.
Keep **savings** in the bank and the paid-off pickup running.
Start looking at a **one-bedroom** to buy.
feel: He feels **calm**, even good, because things stay the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say us lot in the trades are fine, it's the office types who need to worry. At the truck, we'd probably joke about the estimators getting replaced. I wouldn't say anything online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's mostly the office side. They'd use computers to plan our routes and do the quotes, and I'd still be setting poles. Robots spreading slowly means I've got years before anything climbs a pole for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my apprenticeship and not change much. If the office makes us use some new app, I'd use it, grudgingly. I'd put a bit more aside each month, maybe an extra two hundred, just in case the contractor cuts back on office people and loses tenders because of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit irritated by the apps, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at work be worried about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our estimator, Phil, he's in his fifties and he does the job quotes by hand. If a computer does quotes in a minute, he's done. I'd feel bad, he gave me my first chance on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that make you want to learn anything new yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I want to be good at the bit computers can't do, which is the actual climbing and framing. That's where I'm spending my energy.

feel: He feels **mostly calm**, a bit irritated by apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness, honestly, and somebody should slow it down. I'm not a politics person, but two years is too fast for anyone. At the truck we'd be talking about nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's bad for me. Thinking AI by 2028 kills the office, and the contractor might not even need an estimator or a planner. Then robots by 2031. I'm the guy with seven months saved and one trade, and I'd have three years of setting poles before the machines show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop looking at flats to buy, straight away. I'd keep every penny I can, maybe get the savings up to a year. And I'd wait and see what the robots actually look like, because I'm not going to retrain into something I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, I've got money, but I'd be looking at the robots on the news a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see. What would make you act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing one actually set a pole on a street like ours, not in a video. If that happens, I'd start looking at something like heavy equipment or crane work, where you still need a person for a while. Probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your aunt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine for now, and that I might need the flat a bit longer than I planned. She'd be glad, honestly, she likes having me around to fix things.

say: I'd say two years is **too fast** and somebody should slow it down.
I'd talk about **nothing else** at the truck.
think: Privately, **AGI by 2028** could empty the office and cut contractor work.
With **robots by 2031**, he'd have three years of setting poles left.
do: Stop looking at **flats to buy** straight away.
Build savings up to **a full year**.
Wait to see **real robots** before retraining.
feel: He feels **anxious**, though savings keep him from panic.
S2.quote: I'm the guy with seven months saved and one trade, and I'd have three years of setting poles before the machines show up.
fieldNote: He's **resistant** and won't retrain until he sees robots on his own streets.
He names **crane work** as a fallback, without much conviction.
He leans on his **aunt's flat** as a quiet safety net.

Stay longer in the cheap flat above his aunt's garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is quick, but at least we'd see it coming. I'd tell the crew to get their tickets done, because a journeyman's ticket is worth more than an apprentice's when they start cutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gets me my journeyman ticket and a couple of years on top. That helps. But robots at 2034 are still the same problem, just later, and I'd be thirty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship, keep saving, maybe buy a small place but a cheap one. I'd keep an eye on crane and heavy equipment courses, maybe look at what they cost. I wouldn't sign up yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but less. More of a slow worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between anxious here and in the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two-year picture I'd be counting months. With five years I'd be counting years, and I can live with counting years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about the crane idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Dani runs a crane at the port. I'd ask her how long she thinks they'll need people. She'd tell me straight.

I'd tell the crew to get their **journeyman tickets** done.

S3.quote: In the two-year picture I'd be counting months. With five years I'd be counting years, and I can live with counting years.
fieldNote: Time changes his worry from **months to years**.

steps.text: Finish the journeyman ticket on schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so nobody should panic. I'd probably say something like, I'll be a foreman by then, let the robots work for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it someone else's problem for a while. By 2036 I'd be in my late thirties, with a ticket and a house. Robots around 2039 are far enough away that I'd plan for it later, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the one-bedroom, keep the apprenticeship going, keep saving like normal. Maybe in five years I'd look at the crane course or something else. For now, I'd just do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said let the robots work for you. Do you mean that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half-joking. I've no idea how to run a robot. But if someone has to stand there and watch the robots, I'd rather it be someone who knows what a pole is supposed to look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger kid joining the trade in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do it, get your ticket, and save your money like I did. It worked for me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years of office stuff disappearing, then robots three years later, and I'm still learning. What would help is a year of savings and knowing which trades still need people, maybe a list from the trade school, something straight.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the contractors. Private outfits like ours can drop people fast, so if robots come, contractor crews would feel it first. The power company's own crews have more protection.

headlineQuote: Private outfits like ours can drop people fast, so if robots come, contractor crews would feel it first.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old apprentice** with a private line contractor, setting poles in new estates.
He has **seven months saved**, a paid-off pickup, and rents cheaply above his aunt's garage.
He **never uses AI**, keeps a paper notebook, and prefers things as they are.
He stays calm in slow pictures but grows **anxious** when robots could arrive by 2031.
He prefers to **wait and see** rather than retrain, though crane work is his fallback.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with **robots by 2031** while he's still learning the trade.
whatWouldHelp: A full **year** of savings and a straight list of **trades needing people**.
